Nitecore NWL20

Reverse engineering a work light

I disassembled a Nitecore NWL20 work light and recreated its components and assembly in SOLIDWORKS.

Context
MCEN 1025 · April–May 2026
My role
Measurement, CAD & drawings
Tools
SOLIDWORKS, calipers
Deliverables
16 parts · 2 subassemblies · 5 drawings

An educational reverse-engineering project. Nitecore designed the original product. I created the CAD model and engineering drawings shown here.

On this pageProject OverviewMeasurement & ModelingModeling ChallengesEngineering DrawingsResults & Lessons Learned
01 / Overview

Project Overview

I chose this work light because I wanted something I could take apart and learn about while making the model. The NWL20 has a magnetic base and a hinge that rotates through 180 degrees, along with electronics, wiring, and internal mounting features.

02 / Process

Measurement & Modeling

I measured the components with calipers. The electronics and wires made some internal dimensions difficult to access, which made the main housing more challenging to measure.

When I was unsure how to model a feature, stepping back and thinking about its basic geometry helped. I used the rollback bar and feature suppression to try different approaches. The project also gave me practice with fill patterns and draft cuts.

03 / Challenges

Modeling Challenges

The main body was the most difficult part because it had very little symmetry, changing geometry, and many small details. Almost every other component connected to it, so it needed several mounting points that matched the surrounding parts.

Discrepancies between measured and intended dimensions caused some parts to interfere in the assembly. I rechecked the dimensions and adjusted the housing’s mounting features where components collided.

04 / Documentation

Engineering Drawings

The main body was the most difficult drawing because of its limited symmetry, small details, patterns, and threads. I also gained experience with hole tables while creating the drawings.

05 / Results

Results & Lessons Learned

The model has several differences from the original product. The buttons are extruded from the main body rather than modeled as separate parts, and the button pattern is slightly different. I omitted the rubber sealing rings and their grooves, and some material appearances differ from the physical work light.

Trying different modeling techniques took more time than I expected. One of the main lessons was knowing when to stop adding detail, especially for internal pieces that contributed little to the project. The drawings took about as much time as modeling, so I learned to allow enough time for both. I also learned to save frequently.
